blogs.description: TypeSafe AI is an AI lab building machine-native intelligence infrastructure for automation, designed to make decisions within software. Try our first System One Model, Jev, in early access.
blogs.content: Jev: For the builders AND dreamers - TypeSafe AI Blog TypeSafe AI Enterprise Thoughts Company Docs API console Contact us API console Docs Menu ∵ Back Company News Company News Jev: For the builders AND dreamers Oct 14, 2026 Oct 14, 2026 Oct 14, 2026 TL;DR: We're releasing an improved Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for our dreamers: images, a new type, and longer context. Enter the danger zone at your own risk. 🔥 Our philosophy A huge debate we’ve been having is on the balance between reliability and creativity. To really care about the prod builders, we should be shipping models that meet our quality bar for intelligence and have been battle-tested to the limits of what we can do internally. On the other hand, there’s no way that our team has a full understanding of what is needed to spark delight in the world and build sick sci-fi. We don’t want to impose our values of extreme reliability on those dreamers. Our solution: share those dreamer-ready features under “danger zone” flags in our API headers. These are features that will be here to stay for future models, are (as far as we can tell) better than what exists out there, and will continue to get better by leaps and bounds. But as a warning, we think there is still way too much jaggedness for us to vouch for these for production use cases! See these new capabilities as a continuation of what we’ve built over 2 years of stealth. They’re less ready for automation, but very fun to play with. They’re also an early glimpse into what we’re focused on making reliable enough to meet TypeSafe standards. Composable Images Not only are we enabling multimodality for future Jev models, we’re enabling it for the current Jev that you all know and love. Surprise: the Jev you all know and love ( jev-1.13.0 ) was multimodal all along! Image support is fully composable via a find-and-replace in assets . You can put them anywhere that our JSON interface supports: in the state , instructions , or even criteria ! Play around with it, push the boundaries of technology, and let us know where Jev can improve. As a warning, all models (Jev included) perform worse on multimodality over pure text. Breaking down questions into the simplest possible decompositions helps a lot. TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/images Types Beyond Decisions We’re introducing another new type as well: box . It returns a single bounding box - no type errors allowed. It’s our first type that’s not purely meant for smart-if statements, and is a preview for our explorations beyond simple decisions into what else System One Models can support. We made huge leaps and bounds on this one recently, so we’re enabling this only for jev-1.14.0 (spoilers). Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/box Size does matter, apparently 💅 We’ve heard you loud and clear on context lengths. Jev actually supports a much longer context length than we’ve enabled in production. We chose to limit it intentionally because Jev, like all models, is less reliable on longer contexts, and this constraint encourages more effective usage patterns in prod. We aren’t your parents though, so while we strongly recommend limiting context length, you no longer have to: TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/models#context-length Opt-in to help us We love the community’s desire to help make models better! We’ve added an opt-in to allow you to help find model jaggedness with your queries. We will still not train on your queries, but this does make it easier for us to find issues and help debug your use cases. jev-1.14.0 We’re also releasing a new version of Jev under jev-preview ! Not meant to be flashy but instead be small, subtle improvements to everything . Most things should be a tiny bit better, but we expect the largest gain in multi-lingual support. blogs.content: $550M Series E $550M Series E Led by Atreides Management published Oct 21, 2026 Legora raises $550 million Series E at $8.8 billion valuation to accelerate growth. Round led by Atreides with established long-term and strategic investors. Capital funds US and international expansion and further investment in the Legora aOS. NEW YORK & STOCKHOLM, October 21, 2026 – Legora, the agentic operating system for legal professionals, today announced it has raised a $550 million Series E at an $8.8 billion post-money valuation. The round was led by Atreides Management, with participation from new investors, including Baron Capital, Capital Group, Fidelity Management & Research Company, Glade Brook Capital Partners, and J.P Morgan. Every major existing investor, including Accel, Benchmark, Bessemer Venture Partners, General Catalyst, ICONIQ, Insight Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures, Redpoint Ventures, Salesforce Ventures, and Sands Capital, is also participating. Legora built the round around investors with a long time horizon. It brings together established long-term holders with strategic investors, institutions that work with law firms and in-house legal teams every day and have a close view of where legal work is heading. The round follows a period of rapid growth. Legora went from $1 million to $100 million in ARR in less than 18 months, faster than any other enterprise software company selling through a direct sales team, and the next $100 million took less than six months. ARR now stands at more than $200 million. The new valuation compares with $5.6 billion at the company's previous round. Legal teams are moving beyond AI assistants toward agents that carry out multi-step work, and Legora's offering and geographic footprint are expanding to meet that shift. In-house legal teams, only a small fraction of Legora's customer base a year ago, made up more than 40% of new customers in the third quarter. In the United States, now Legora's largest market by revenue, more than half of the AmLaw 50 are customers, and Legora opened its first US office only in spring 2025. "The opportunity in legal is enormous and we are still early. AI is changing the role of the lawyer, with more time for judgment and advice, and it is reshaping how law firms and in-house legal teams are organized and how their work gets done. We intend to lead that shift in the US and globally. We chose investors who share our long-term view and know what it takes to build a lasting company. They are the right partners for the years ahead," said Max Junestrand, CEO and Co-Founder of Legora. The capital will support continued expansion in North America, where Legora has offices in New York, Denver, Chicago, Houston, San Francisco, Toronto and Mexico City, as well as in its markets across Europe and Asia-Pacific. It will also deepen investment in the Legora aOS, the agentic operating system that lawyers and their agents work in; bringing new products like agentic in-take, horizon scanning and legal research to life. "Legal is a sophisticated market with demanding buyers, and the bar for software is high. Legora has become the platform that law firms and in-house legal teams adopt and then expand across their organizations, and it has done so while growing at remarkable speed. Legora has also built a sustainable business along the way, with the discipline to scale fast and stay efficient. We are excited to support the team as Legora enters its next stage of growth in the US and globally," said Gavin Baker, Managing Partner and CIO at Atreides. Legora was founded in 2023, and launched its platform in October 2024. It now has more than 1,000 employees across 18 offices and is used by more than 140,000 legal professionals at more than 2,400 leading law firms and in-house legal teams across over 80 markets. Scaling fast, built to last. Category Legora voices published Oct 23, 2026 author Max Junestrand When I started Legora with my co-founders, we made a rule: every new customer had to make the company stronger. It goes back to our partnership with Mannheimer Swartling, one of the largest firms in the Nordics, and our first big customer. We built the product alongside their lawyers, setting up Legora's first office in one of their conference rooms, and we have built it with our customers ever since. Three years on we have more than 2,400 customers, and the rule hasn’t changed. Each one made the product better and the economics healthier. That way of working is the main reason we’ve come this far, and a large part of why we can announce a $550 million Series E this week, at an $8.8 billion post-money valuation, led by Atreides Management. Here is how we got here. Who we raised from New investors include Baron Capital, Fidelity Management & Research Company, Glade Brook Capital Partners, and J.P Morgan. We built this round around those who plan to be with us for the long-game, and every major existing investor, the ones who’ve seen us up close, chose to back us again. We raised with significant cash still in the bank. Our growth doesn’t depend on outside capital, but this round lets us go faster. How we run Legora We build on the best frontier models, and don’t train our own general legal model. That was a real debate when we started in 2023. The models were new, and plenty of people said the way to win in legal AI was to fine-tune your own. We didn’t have the money for it, and fine-tuning didn’t seem to work at our scale. Training a new generation of model costs billions, and most of what lawyers needed wasn’t in the model anyway. It was in everything around it: security, privacy, parsing, working with large sets of documents. So we bet on every frontier model and put our effort into making them work for lawyers. Since then a better, cheaper model has arrived every few months. We build boats, not houses: when the models rise, everything we’ve built floats higher. Legora routes each task to the model that does it best, and we only post-train for narrow jobs where frontier models fall short. That bet also made us efficient. We invested early in model routing and benchmarking. Every new model goes through our own evaluations before it touches customer work, so we know exactly where it’s strong, and each task goes to the model that does it best. Customers get better performance at lower cost, and Legora has always run at a positive gross margin, one that keeps improving. We build Legora together with our customers, and we wanted our pricing to reflect that. We get paid when customers get value. We were the first large legal AI company to offer consumption-based pricing, so what a customer pays rises and falls with the work Legora does for them. We only grow with a customer when Legora is earning its place, which keeps our interests pointed the same way. It’s the rule we started with, written into how we charge. To keep earning that place, we do more than ship software. Building technology is hard. Changing how a law firm works is harder. So when we launched, we didn’t hand lawyers a product and wish them luck. We had former lawyers ready to sit with them and show how it fit their practice area. We call them legal engineers. We now employ more than 150, and they work inside customer teams on their hardest matters. One of them once flew from New York to Stockholm on a Saturday and spent a week and a half with our engineers. A large US firm wanted to switch to us, but needed one specific task solved, and we couldn’t do it yet. He built it. That is what we mean by partner. We now have more lawyers than software engineers. blogs.content: Linklaters and Legora: building the firm-wide standard for agentic AI | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Resources Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Linklaters and Legora: building the firm-wide standard for agentic AI Linklaters and Legora: building the firm-wide standard for agentic AI Category published Oct 22, 2026 author Team Legora Over the past year, Linklaters, one of the world's largest law firms, has redefined its ways of working around the Legora Agent. The impact has been transformational. Within a month of rollout, 97% of weekly active users were working in the Agent. Combined, Linklaters' lawyers around the world have now spent over 35 years on the platform since deployment. Kris Sales, Product Owner for Legora, says, “I don't think we've ever had a technology product become so popular so quickly.” Kris has been involved with Legora since the very first conversations, through the proof of concept, the deployment, and now day-to-day operation. Alongside him, Tom Quoroll and Sarah Barnard sit at the centre of Linklaters' relationship with Legora. Together they steer the firm's AI strategy, work that covers everything from tool rollouts to the strategic questions AI raises about the firm’s business model and how it trains the lawyers of the future. As one of the world’s largest law firms, Linklaters is often engaged by clients on highly complex matters that span multiple legal jurisdictions. That means the opportunity to take advantage of the benefits of AI is a global one, and Legora has been rolled out across Linklaters’ firm-wide as a result, but it also makes the work around adoption and the partnership with technology providers even more important. In their roles, Tom and Sarah are thinking deeply about how AI is deployed and adopted effectively and responsibly across Linklaters, as well as assessing the granular matter level data to understand when and where AI is being used to deliver benefits – both areas where the partnership with Legora has paid dividends. On the frontline of client delivery, the pair also recently founded Applied Intelligence, a new practice group bringing data scientists and lawyers together under one roof to work on clients’ most complex problems. Sarah is Linklaters’ Director of AI Delivery, responsible for taking that strategy and transferring it into a credible working practice, with measurable growth to show for it month on month. As Tom puts it: “Between the three of us, you have the team required to transform a law firm. We're each bringing different parts of the puzzle.” The impact of the partnership Firm-wide weekly active use rose almost 15% since the Legora Agent was rolled out, against a user base that expanded faster still (growing by approximately 20%) as Legora was adopted more widely across the firm. Partner engagement strengthened over the same period: monthly active partners rose from 65% to almost 80%, which is one of the fastest partner adoption ramps either Linklaters or Legora has seen. Monthly adoption of the Legora Agent now stands at 70%. Working closely with Legora’s Legal Engineers, Tom, Sarah and Kris have turned a technology rollout into a genuine change in how the firm operates. Here’s how they achieved it. A peer-led approach to adoption When the Linklaters team started evaluating AI platforms, they had already worked through two rounds of AI tooling. This meant the firm went into the process focused less on demos and more on how the right platform would actually feel in a lawyer's hands. “We had quite a high bar to start from in some ways,” says Kris, “because our users knew what they wanted.” When Legora reached those users, the feedback came back fast. “It was a much simpler interface, they just got on with it better,” says Kris. blogs.title: How Law Firms Turn AI Efficiency Into Client Value
blogs.author: Harvey Team
blogs.description: Faster legal work raises a bigger question for firms: How can they turn time saved into better outcomes for their clients?
blogs.content: Insights How Law Firms Turn AI Efficiency Into Client Value Faster legal work raises a bigger question for firms: How can they turn time saved into better outcomes for their clients? by Harvey Team • Oct 23, 2026 AI is changing how quickly law firms can complete legal work. For clients, though, it’s about what that speed makes possible: an earlier business decision, a broader view of risk, or more time for the judgment a matter requires. At Harvey FORUM in Sydney, Hilary Goodier (Partner and Global Chair of NewLaw and Consulting at Ashurst Perkins Coie) and Michelle Mahoney (Chief Innovation Officer at Mallesons) were joined by Michael Griffith (Deputy General Counsel at Telstra) for a candid discussion of how AI is changing the value firms can deliver, and how clients assess it. Their perspectives offer a way for law firms and legal teams to think more clearly about pricing, service, and the time lawyers spend on the work that is more valuable. Show Clients What AI Changes Clients want to see what a firm’s use of AI changes about the work they receive. Griffith said Telstra, Australia’s leading telecommunications and information services company, evaluates firms on the same things it valued before AI — what has changed is the range of benefits a firm might be able to deliver. Watch Video His questions give firms a useful starting point when discussing a matter with a client. Could AI reduce the cost of the work? Help the firm deliver specialized advice sooner? Make it possible to examine more documents or identify risks that would otherwise go unexplored? The answer will depend on what the client is trying to achieve. A deadline tied to a business decision, for example, may make speed more valuable than a reduction in fees. That distinction is important when firms decide how to scope and price the work. The most compelling proposal is one that explains what the client will gain and how the firm plans to deliver it. Connect Faster Work to Client Value The value of faster work depends on what clients can do with the time gained. Goodier described an obligations mapping project for a global investment bank that her team completed in five weeks using AI, compared with an estimated six months by conventional methods. The client estimated that the work would allow it to enter a new market five months earlier. Watch Video Goodier said the firm spoke openly with the client about what the project needed to achieve and how to share the value created by using AI. In this case, the earlier market entry mattered more than the reduction in legal fees. On another matter, lower costs or a more thorough review might be the priority. Those differences are hard to reflect in a standard discount applied to every AI-assisted task. They also raise a question for firms built around billable hours. When a firm can deliver valuable work in much less time, an hourly fee may no longer reflect what the client receives or what it takes the firm to deliver it. Watch Video Changing the price is only part of the challenge. Goodier noted that targets and bonuses tied to hours can discourage lawyers from using methods that save time. Firms need to consider how they recognize that work internally if they want lawyers to deliver using AI consistently. Make Room for Deeper Analysis AI can also change the scope of the work a firm is able to offer. Mahoney described how her team now spends less time gathering and organizing data, leaving more time to examine what it reveals. Watch Video When lawyers spend less time gathering the data, they can examine more of it and ask questions that a narrower review might miss. Mahoney gave the example of examining a clause across thousands of arrangements, rather than looking at a small sample. Goodier pointed to contract remediation, portfolio reviews, and compliance projects that clients may previously have considered too expensive or time-consuming to pursue. blogs.title: What Does a Regulator Look for in Your Notice of Violation Response?
blogs.author: Harvey Team
blogs.description: What regulators look for in a notice of violation response, from FDA Form 483s to OSHA citations and Wells notices, and how to build the record first.
blogs.content: Insights What Does a Regulator Look for in Your Notice of Violation Response? What regulators look for in a notice of violation response, from FDA Form 483s to OSHA citations and Wells notices, and how to build the record first. by Harvey Team • Oct 22, 2026 A regulatory notice of violation means a regulator has looked at an organization's operations, practices, or conduct and found a potential compliance problem. Depending on the procedure, the organization may need to contest the finding, state its position, describe corrective actions taken or planned, or respond within a set period. The same phrase shows up on parking tickets and local code citations, but a regulatory finding needs its own response discipline. If your team is still interpreting new rules, regulatory change management comes first. This article walks through what starts after that work has run and a regulator has still found something. AI speeds up the first stage of the response. Harvey, for example, can help build the chronology and evidence index, test the finding against the record, and draft the first response pack. Your team spends its time on the position instead of on assembling the file. In the US, findings come from regulators such as the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA). The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and transportation security and nuclear regulators issue them, too. Elsewhere, a finding can arrive as a tax authority inquiry or a notice to produce from a workplace regulator. The document differs, but the response discipline stays the same. Examples of regulatory notices include: Notice Who Issues it What the Response Usually Involves FDA Form 483 FDA investigators, at the close of an inspection A voluntary written response, recommended within 15 business days, addressing each observation and any corrective actions taken or planned OSHA citation OSHA A written notice of contest within 15 working days if the employer contests. An informal conference can be requested in that window, but it doesn't extend the deadline SEC Wells notice SEC enforcement staff An optional Wells submission, written or by video, arguing why the Commission should not bring an action. The SEC ordinarily allows four weeks EPA notice of violation EPA A written response and corrective steps, with terms set by the statute involved While the procedures differ, every response has to hold up to an adversarial reader, match the record behind it, and survive the commitments it makes. The Response is Read Adversarially A response to a regulatory finding is a formal submission, and the regulator reads it against the facts already on record. Reviewers look for omitted information, statements that don't match the documents, and characterizations that flatter the facts beyond what the evidence supports. While you prepare the response, keep three things distinct: The response and its commitments. This is the formal submission, setting out the organization's position on the finding and any remediation it commits to. The factual record. These are the documents and other evidence that establish what happened and support each factual assertion in the response. Internal deliberations and legal analysis. These shape how the organization evaluates the finding. Depending on how particular communications were created and shared, attorney-client privilege or work-product protection may apply, so counsel should assess privilege and waiver before anything is disclosed. Whether a response or the material behind it can later be obtained, admitted, or used elsewhere depends on the regulator, the procedure, the jurisdiction, and the protections that apply. Every factual assertion needs a source in the file, and dates have to reconcile across the correspondence, the supporting documents, and the final submission. blogs.title: How We Made Review Tables Faster and More Reliable
blogs.author: Shrihari Murlidharan
blogs.description: Harvey engineers redesigned Review Table loading for reviews spanning thousands of documents, fetching rows page by page so large tables open faster and stay responsive.
blogs.content: Technical How We Made Review Tables Faster and More Reliable Harvey engineers redesigned Review Table loading for reviews spanning thousands of documents, fetching rows page by page so large tables open faster and stay responsive. by Shrihari Murlidharan and Stella Ge • Oct 22, 2026 The Review Table is Harvey’s largest, most exhaustive inference engine, allowing users to analyze thousands of legal documents and standardize insights using natural language. Lawyers can ask questions against uploaded documents and obtain the results in a structured tabular format, with rows corresponding to individual documents and columns mapping to the questions. Each cell answer includes the model’s reasoning and is backed by citations from the source document. Review Tables are also designed to be a living, collaborative surface: rows can be assigned out to collaborators for review, answers can be verified or locked, and users can leave comments for further discussion. Once verified, teams can lean on their review table as a reusable, validated source of truth for their next memo or presentation without needing to recreate their insights from scratch. That collaborative workflow depends on the table remaining responsive as it grows. As teams began querying hundreds of columns across thousands of files, loading the full table in the browser caused delays and, in the largest cases, could prevent it from loading at all. This post explains how we changed the table’s data and loading paths to support larger reviews while preserving sorting and filtering. When Browser Loading Hit its Limits Historically, all table operations were performed on the client side. The browser loaded the entire Review Table from the blob store and performed sorting, filtering, and any sort of aggregation in-memory. While this solution worked for small Review Tables, we saw performance issues once the table exceeded thousands of rows. When Review Tables adoption and usage skyrocketed, we saw that tables sometimes experienced lag times or became unresponsive. For extremely large tables, browsers could potentially run out of memory or fail to load entirely. It may seem like solving this scaling problem is straightforward. Since it’s a table data structure at its core, we should be able to address this problem by implementing server-side pagination. In reality, there’s two main things that prevent this fix: The requirement to segregate sensitive data . Client data at Harvey is extremely sensitive and as such, only the metadata lives in Postgres while raw customer data lives in Azure blobs. The data had to be fetched from Azure at request time, merged with Postgres data, and passed from the backend to the client. In order to support server-side pagination with filtering and sorting, we would need an interface to query on top of Azure blob store. There is no existing grid library that supports the kind of pagination scheme this would require . As a result, we had to come up with our own abstractions for page loading strategy, factoring in grouping by folder path, sorting, and filtering. In order to ensure this implementation achieved parity with our existing features, we built our own versions of table functionality for row selection and expanding/collapsing sections that we no longer got for free from our current grid library. How We Implemented Pagination Choosing a data store In order to scale the user interface, we moved all client side operations to the server side. This necessitated a reliable data store that both satisfied our segregation requirements and exposed a rich querying interface with aggregation. Postgres would still be our source of truth while the new data store would provide the read interface (CQRS pattern). Turbopuffer is a vector data store that runs on top of existing Azure blobs while supporting vector search (ANN, KNN), full text search (BM25), and straightforward filtering through an inverted index. blogs.description: Teach the Agent how you work. Skills let legal teams encode their standards, processes and preferences inside the Legora aOS™.
blogs.content: The ten-year head start: How Stewart McKelvey got ready for AI before it arrived | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Resources Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Shapers The ten-year head start: How Stewart McKelvey got ready for AI before it arrived The ten-year head start: How Stewart McKelvey got ready for AI before it arrived Category Shapers published Oct 13, 2026 author Team Legora Lydia Bugden and Paul Saunders have spent more than a decade pursuing a shared vision for Stewart McKelvey, just from different seats. As CEO and Managing Partner, Lydia oversees the firm's six offices in Atlantic Canada, more than 250 lawyers, and over 350 staff on any given day. As Chief Strategy and Innovation Officer and Partner, Paul co-chairs the firm's AI and Technology Steering Committee, drives strategy and innovation across the firm, and is now Managing Director of Stewart McKelvey’s newest venture: the Fortified Firm. Eleven years ago, the two of them made the case to the firm's partnership board for something no one at Stewart McKelvey had done before: a dedicated practice innovation function. Its job was to systematically improve how the firm practiced law, covering everything from process and pricing to technology and profitability. They made that call years before generative AI existed, which is largely why the firm was ready to move fast once AI arrived to the business of law in a substantive way. Two different starting points, one shared instinct Lydia's path to leadership ran through in-house roles first. Those years gave her an early look at how good businesses are run, rather than just the legal work layered on top of them. Sitting on the client side meant understanding different law firms' value for herself, and taking on project work that stretched beyond legal advice into the operational side of the business. "They always let me do a little bit more than just the law," she says. "And I enjoyed that quite a bit." She became CEO and Managing Partner in August 2015, and has since been balancing the collegiality of a partnership alongside the discipline of running Atlantic Canada’s largest law firm. Early on, she pushed back when a senior partner insisted the firm was a partnership, not a business, telling him they were "professionals in a big business." This ability to see what's working ‘under the hood’ is what took her from evaluating outside counsel to running a substantial business. Paul came to law with a background in finance and technology. "I just started to look at opportunities to systematize, improve processes, solve problems," he says, recalling his first summer at work. Lydia noticed early. "Paul was the young lawyer you'd have someone pitch a virtual data room to for 50,000 US dollars," she says, "and he'd come in on a Monday and say, if you don't mind, I spent 18 dollars on a license, and here's a secure data room we can use. He'd solve the problem, but he'd also build something everyone else at the firm could use." By his fifth or sixth year practicing, Paul took a secondment to work on technology projects, and a trip to a legal conference in Chicago sharpened his sense of urgency. "I just couldn't believe what some of the conversations about profitability and leverage and pricing were, things we just weren't exploring at that point," he says. He came back and, in the fall of 2015, not long after Lydia became CEO, the two of them flew to St. John's to pitch creating a practice innovation role to the partnership board. Paul left his practice to become the firm's first Practice Innovation Partner, building out document automation, process mapping, and checklists. "It wasn't a hard sell," Lydia says. "Paul said he wanted to devote 100 percent of his time to the firm, and it just mushroomed from there." blogs.author: Dominic Ferullo
blogs.description: From advising on decisions earlier to building legal guidance into everyday workflows, Harvey Innovation Partner Dominic Ferullo explores how AI is impacting Legal’s contribution.
blogs.content: Insights How AI is Expanding Legal’s Role Across the Business From advising on decisions earlier to building legal guidance into everyday workflows, Harvey Innovation Partner Dominic Ferullo explores how AI is impacting Legal’s contribution. by Dominic Ferullo • Oct 22, 2026 When I managed an in-house rollout of Harvey at NBCUniversal, I had two workflow imperatives: how could AI help our legal team get involved earlier in business decisions and how could we make our legal guidance easier for teams across the company to use? For us, that might’ve meant being brought into the creative and dealmaking processes that drive the entertainment industry. Now, as an Innovation Partner at Harvey, those same imperatives are front of mind for legal teams I work with across many industries. Legal teams are balancing a steady flow of requests with the need to advise while business decisions are still taking shape. AI can take on parts of high-volume work such as first-pass review, redlines, research, and regulatory monitoring, giving lawyers more room for judgment-heavy advice. The choices leaders make about that added capacity, including where Legal gets involved, what work it takes on, and how its guidance reaches colleagues, shape how the function contributes across the company. That contribution also often includes helping the company decide how to adopt AI more broadly. As AI moves into more functions, legal leaders are increasingly asked to guide rollout, governance, and measurement. Their experience applying AI within Legal gives them a practical perspective to bring to those decisions. Put New Capacity to Work When legal teams use AI, faster turnaround is often the first result the business notices. RSGI’s latest report , based on a survey of 25 in-house Harvey customers, found that 92% of respondents reported faster turnaround to the business. The same survey found that 88% of respondents said they spend more time with the business on higher-value work. blogs.content: Insights A Clause Library Built From Signed Deals Should Shape Every Contract Review What a clause library should include, how to build one from contracts you've already signed, and how to keep it current so lawyers use it. by Harvey Team • Oct 21, 2026 You may have a carefully curated clause library, and when the next agreement arrives, it goes unopened. Lawyers pull old contracts, search for precedents, or ask a colleague what the team usually accepts. The problem is rarely the quality of the language inside the library. A clause library is a governed collection of your organization's approved contract language, organized by clause type. Its value depends on how it connects to review. The library stores the language, and a playbook applies the team's approved positions and escalation rules when the language on the page isn't yours. If the language itself needs work, start with drafting the clause language . This article is about the library as an asset, meaning how you build it, keep it current, and put it to work. A well-maintained library can feed a playbook that runs against incoming paper, give you a benchmark for a single clause against your own deal history, or support a new agreement. Each of those is its own workflow, and whichever you use, the library has to connect its stored positions to the decisions lawyers make before it changes what gets signed. A Clause Library is Only as Useful as the Moment it is Consulted A clause library usually gets consulted at drafting, when a lawyer already knows the position they want. If an agreement needs an indemnity provision, they use the clause taxonomy to find the approved language and draft from there. Review is harder. The counterparty's indemnity language differs from yours without necessarily being unacceptable, and the lawyer has to decide whether it's close enough to a position the organization will accept. A library built around one approved exemplar falls short here. It shows what the organization prefers, but the lawyer also needs to know whether similar language was accepted before, which fallbacks were negotiated, and which deviations were approved and why. If you own the library, the usage data may already show this. Making negotiating history accessible is a core part of legal knowledge management , and a library that leaves lawyers digging through executed agreements or a separate precedent bank gets bypassed. It also makes consistent positions across matters harder to hold. A library can show the range of positions without capturing the tolerance around them: which positions stay acceptable in which circumstances, and when a deviation needs a different response. The Difference Between Stored Language and an Applied Standard A playbook supplies that tolerance. It attaches a preferred position, an acceptable fallback, and an escalation trigger to each clause. When counterparty language departs from the preferred position, the reviewer can see whether it matches a fallback or crosses the threshold. This is the long answer. Between the MCP and better frontier models, agents now run whole design projects end to end across our brand, product marketing, and design work. Here’s what that looks like, and the systems underneath it. Building a Launch Film With Agents Watch Video We made this launch film for Harvey Artifacts entirely with agents, inside of Figma. The agent built every scene as a Figma Motion frame, keyed every camera move, UI state, and line of type on its timeline, and exported the cuts straight from the file. It all started with a storyboard, which is to a film what a PRD is to code: it sits between the creative brief and production, so every shot, line, and transition is decided up front. That forces the model, and us, to be deliberate about every choice. We review on the canvas, sometimes 50 comments at a time. The agent reworks the board after each pass and asks which notes should become rules. For music, we marked where the beat should drop and it retimed every scene to the track. When the ending fell flat, it cut and EQ’d the track, added sound design, and laid out four or five ways the outro could land. Figure 1. The Artifacts storyboard in Figma. Each version is a full board of labeled scenes, with side studies for the ending and the “Share the Work” beat. Tailoring a Demo for Every Account Anyone can get one flashy demo out of an agent. The hard part is scale, so we picked a sales problem: a tailored product film for each of the hundreds of accounts we want to win. Our first prompts came back half decent, and 15 to 20 minutes of back-and-forth got each one into shape. But that wouldn’t scale. So we set out to build a strong foundation in Figma, in two parts. Agents crawled the whole app, clicked every button, and rebuilt all key screens as components, which became Product Map. Then, in Figma Motion, they worked out the grammar of a product film, from camera pushes to screen handoffs to a steady click rhythm, which became Motion Primitives. Both are covered below. With both in place, we worked with the agent to build a menu of 44 company-agnostic demo flows, each built around one moment buyers ask to see, like a playbook redline in Word. For each account, agents use Enterpret's MCP to pull together Gong calls, Salesforce win-loss reports, and Slack. An agent then writes the script, with a fictional company on screen, and voices it as Ashleigh Whittaker, our narrator, whose voice we built in ElevenLabs from ten minutes of her footage. Figure 2. The demo menu in Figma: 44 flows in 13 categories, from Contract Work and Litigation to Memory and Word and Outlook, with one of the sticky notes Shawn and Claude used to work through changes. Making Hundreds Overnight An engine of about 750 lines of JavaScript turns each script into a film inside Figma. Each film is a short list of beats, and the engine handles the camera, transitions, captions, the pointer’s click rhythm, and the end card. Then it lays out contact sheets of the finished film and flags clipped text, small type, and stray pointers, so the obvious mistakes are caught before anyone watches. Lots of small things pop up at scale. Like only one agent can work in a file at a time, so agents queuing in one shared file pushed calls to two minutes and timed out. We built a bus to run them in parallel: three lane files, each with its own builder agent, plus a coordinator for export, mixing, and delivery. AI can help them meet that challenge by expanding capacity, improving response times, and giving lawyers more time to focus on strategy and client service. Turning that potential into firmwide adoption, however, requires an approach that fits the firm’s people, culture, and priorities. One Problem, Different Paths looks at the different tactics legal organizations use to address a shared challenge with Harvey. In this first installment, Munck Wilson Mandala, Gray Reed, and Foley Hoag show how technical fluency, practitioner-led change, and peer learning can each provide a foundation for firmwide AI adoption. Munck Wilson Mandala: Build on the Firm’s Existing Strengths Munck Wilson Mandala began its rollout with a level of technical fluency already embedded in the firm. Roughly half of its nearly 100 lawyers hold STEM degrees, and Managing Partner Bill Munck coded neural networks before attending law school. The firm had also assembled a multidisciplinary group to evaluate AI before generative AI gained widespread attention in the legal industry. That foundation helped Munck Wilson Mandala assess the technology rigorously and identify where it could make the greatest impact. After selecting Harvey, the firm focused on document-intensive work across transactional and litigation practices. It also treated adoption as part of its service to clients. Its AI use policy requires lawyers to communicate openly with clients and obtain their permission, giving clients visibility into how the technology supports their matters. From there, the firm turned early results into broader confidence, including among its clients. When one skeptical general counsel agreed to let the Munck Wilson Mandala team test Harvey on a due diligence project, the team uploaded the relevant contracts, refined its prompts over half a day, and generated an Excel spreadsheet answering every due diligence question. The output achieved more than 90% accuracy, and the firm completed the project in a fraction of the usual time. “ What we did with those contracts would have been three associates working a week and a half. We did it in a day. ” Bill Munck Managing Partner at Munck Wilson Mandala The firm carried that momentum into other areas. In a banking dispute, Dallas Managing Partner Jenny Martinez used Harvey to review a 2,000-page loan file and assemble a timeline, and Harvey surfaced the relevant documents and assembled the timeline in seconds. Associates also use Harvey as a training tool, validating their analysis and identifying what they may have missed before their work reaches a partner. Applying Harvey to both client matters and associate training helped make it part of the firm’s day-to-day work. blogs.title: How to Implement and Track a Litigation Hold Across Every Custodian
blogs.author: Harvey Team
blogs.description: Learn how to implement a litigation hold, track custodian compliance, handle scope changes, and support a defensible preservation process.
blogs.content: Insights How to Implement and Track a Litigation Hold Across Every Custodian Learn how to implement a litigation hold, track custodian compliance, handle scope changes, and support a defensible preservation process. by Harvey Team • Oct 20, 2026 A litigation hold is easy to treat as a communication task. Identifying the right employees, sending a notice, and collecting responses. The harder work starts after that as custodians change roles, new data sources surface, claims evolve, and the legal team still needs to be able to show what the organization asked people to preserve and how that scope changed over time. To implement a litigation hold effectively, legal teams need a repeatable way to define scope, map custodians to relevant systems, issue matter-specific instructions, document follow-up, resolve exceptions, and release the hold when the preservation obligation ends. The goal isn’t paperwork for its own sake, it’s a record that lets counsel explain what the organization did, when it did it, and why. This article focuses on that full lifecycle. For a deeper look at the notice itself, our previous guide to drafting a matter-specific litigation hold notice covers how to turn the triggering matter and preservation scope into instructions employees can act on. A Litigation Hold is an Ongoing Preservation Process, Not a One-Time Notice A litigation hold is a written directive to preserve potentially relevant information , but the directive sits inside a broader preservation process. In U.S. federal litigation, the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure address the loss of electronically stored information (ESI) that should’ve been preserved in anticipation or conduct of litigation. A useful benchmark is the HHS litigation hold policy , which requires the agency to identify custodians, track confirmations, revise scope, send reminders, document newly discovered information or custodians, and communicate when a hold is lifted. Private organizations use different procedures, but the consistent thread is that preservation has to be managed over time. That’s also why both under-preservation and over-preservation can create problems. A scope that’s too narrow can miss evidence, while a scope that’s too broad can freeze large amounts of data that later have to be collected, processed, and reviewed. Good hold management keeps the scope tied to the matter as it develops. 1. Define What the Litigation Hold Actually Needs to Preserve Start with the facts that triggered the preservation duty, not with the template. Counsel should identify the claims or issues that are reasonably in play, the events they turn on, the relevant time period, and the types of information that could affect those questions. A practical initial scope should answer four questions: What issues matter? Which people are likely to have relevant information? Which systems or repositories may contain it? What date range is reasonably connected to the dispute? Those answers give the hold a working boundary and make the later notice more specific. However, the first scope is not necessarily the final scope. New allegations, interviews, document review, or discovery can surface additional custodians or sources. Treat the initial scope as a reasoned starting point that counsel can revisit instead of a fixed list created on day one. 2. Build a Custodian and Data-Source Map Before Sending the Hold Once the legal team knows what information might matter, the next step is to map who’s likely to control it and where it lives. This is where a generic employee list becomes a matter-specific custodian map. Identify the People Who May Control Relevant Information The obvious custodians are the people directly involved in the events at issue, but the list often extends beyond them. Managers, employees copied on key communications, IT or records personnel, former employees, departing employees, and appropriate third parties may all control information that matters to the case. The initial

blogs.content: KI im Rechtsbereich: Was Teams heute brauchen | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Resources Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Perspectives KI im Rechtsbereich: Was Teams heute brauchen KI im Rechtsbereich: Was Teams heute brauchen Category Perspectives published Oct 13, 2026 author Janusch Krasberg Anfang 2026 arbeiteten rund 3.000 Juristinnen und Juristen in Deutschland mit Legora. Bei der Eröffnung des Münchner Büros Ende September waren es bereits mehr als 13.000. Besonders stark wächst die Nutzung in Rechtsabteilungen: Dort hat sich die Zahl der Nutzenden seit Januar verachtfacht. Deutschland hat den Ruf, neue Technologien eher zögerlich aufzugreifen. Bei KI zeichnet sich ein anderes Bild ab: Kanzleien und Rechtsabteilungen setzen die Technologie mit bemerkenswertem Tempo ein. Für den deutschen Markt reicht es nicht, KI ins Deutsche zu übersetzen. Sie muss auf das deutsche Recht und die Arbeitsweise juristischer Teams ausgerichtet sein. In unseren Gesprächen mit Kanzleien und Rechtsabteilungen in Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz verändern sich die Fragen. In ersten Tests von KI-Lösungen für den Rechtsbereich ging es vor allem darum, wie verlässlich KI bei Recherche, Analyse und Entwürfen unterstützt. Inzwischen beschäftigen sich die Teams zunehmend mit der Auswahl eines passenden Anbieters, der Einführung im Team und der Einbindung in bestehende Arbeitsabläufe. Bei der Auswahl einer passenden Lösung zeigt sich in intensiven Pilotphasen, wie gut sie zum eigenen Arbeitsalltag passt. Teams bringen dafür ihre vorhandenen Unterlagen, ihr Wissen und ihre internen Vorgaben ein. Entscheidend ist, wie gut Legora diese Informationen nutzbar macht und sich an die Arbeitsweise des jeweiligen Teams anpasst: wie Ergebnisse aufbereitet werden, wie sie in die weitere Beratung einfließen und wie Kolleginnen und Kollegen damit zusammenarbeiten. Was deutsche juristische Arbeit von KI verlangt Wer Rechts-KI in Deutschland einführt, trifft auf konkrete fachliche Anforderungen. Das beginnt bei der Sprache. Eine juristische Stellungnahme auf Deutsch muss Fachbegriffe präzise verwenden, die relevante Fragestellung erfassen und eine nachvollziehbare Argumentation enthalten. Bei grenzüberschreitenden Mandaten kommen unterschiedliche Arbeitssprachen hinzu. Ein englischsprachiger Vertrag kann die Grundlage für eine deutsche Stellungnahme bilden, die anschließend mit einem internationalen Team abgestimmt wird. Eigene Vertragsmuster und frühere Stellungnahmen ermöglichen es Teams, Entwürfe in Legora an den fachlichen und sprachlichen Standards ihrer Organisation auszurichten. Ebenso entscheidend sind die Rechtsquellen. Gesetze, Rechtsprechung und Kommentarliteratur bilden zusammen mit dem Wissen der jeweiligen Organisation die Grundlage juristischer Arbeit. Für KI-Anwendungen bedeutet das: Der Zugang zu relevanten Inhalten, erkennbare Fundstellen und die Möglichkeit zur Überprüfung müssen im Arbeitsablauf mitgedacht werden. Deutsche Fachverlage spielen deshalb auch bei der Entwicklung von Rechts-KI eine wichtige Rolle. Wer Module von Otto Schmidt abonniert hat, kann diese direkt in Legora nutzen. Hinzu kommt der Umgang mit Daten. Kanzleien und Unternehmen benötigen konkrete Antworten darauf, wo Informationen verarbeitet werden, wer darauf zugreifen kann und wie ihre Verwendung geregelt ist. Datensouveränität und Vertraulichkeit gehören damit an den Anfang der Einführung. Wer Rechts-KI für Deutschland auswählt, sollte ihre Qualität an deutscher juristischer Arbeit messen. Gute Ergebnisse im britischen oder US-amerikanischen Rechtskontext lassen sich nicht ohne Weiteres übertragen. Kanzleien und Rechtsabteilungen sollten deshalb anhand eigener Fälle prüfen, ob eine Lösung relevante deutsche Quellen einbezieht, juristische Begriffe präzise verwendet und ihre Ergebnisse nachvollziehbar belegt. Ebenso muss sie die Anforderungen der Organisation an Vertraulichkeit und Zusammenarbeit erfüllen. Wie Rechtsabteilungen ihren KI-Einsatz weite

blogs.description: Spellbook Labs analyzed 3,000+ public-company agreements across 520 organizations. Sixty percent had drafting errors.
blogs.content: 60% of SEC-Filed Contracts Contain Errors | Spellbook Labs spellbook.legal cookie bridge --> Overview Findings at a Glance Issues by Company Issues by Founding Decade Issues by Industry Issues by Contract Type Issues by Filing Year Conclusion Methodology and Scope Humans Hallucinate Too Humans Hallucinate Too. 60% of SEC-Filed Contracts Contain Errors Spellbook Labs analyzed 60,000 pages of public-company agreements across 520 organizations. Sixty percent of contracts had drafting errors. When a self-driving car crashes, it makes the news. The scrutiny is warranted, but the headlines obscure the baseline. Human drivers cause far more crashes . They happen every day, yet almost none become media stories. In legal work, AI hallucinations also get the headlines. An AI-generated legal brief citing non-existent case studies. A judge who used AI to create a restraining order and misquoted state law. These are real issues that deserve attention. But Spellbook sees a different side to AI’s impact on legal and contract workflow. We see the human mistakes that are made when volume and complexity are met with limited hours and manual review. In fact, our data shows saved hours, greater accuracy and increased output when AI is deployed. So we decided to dig into the data to prove what we already know intuitively—humans make mistakes too. Using Spellbook Reviews, we analyzed 3,000+ SEC-filed contracts from over 500 companies, spanning 22 years. These were executed agreements from some of the largest and most heavily lawyered companies in the world. The findings showed plenty of interesting trends and fun examples. Six in ten contracts contained drafting issues. Many were minor. But one in 40 was high-risk—defined as changing the meaning of an agreement in a substantially negative way for at least one party—and they were concentrated in provisions that decide who gets paid, who carries the liability, and what happens in a dispute. None of this is a matter of carelessness by lawyers so much as a consequence of the length, complexity, and disjointed nature of how these types of SEC-filed agreements are prepared and negotiated. In this context, mistakes are inevitable. But they don’t have to be. Every company, public or private, will eventually run its contracts through products like Spellbook that will not only spot errors and risks immediately but suggest fixes based on a company’s own agreement context and real-time market data. Issue Example: A loan cap written two different ways. A mining company's loan agreement set its borrowing limit at "One Million Five-Hundred Sixty Thousand Dollars," then printed the figure beside it as $1,750,000.00. The words and the number differ by $190,000, and the mismatch appears twice. If the borrower and lender ever disagree, the contract gives a court no clear answer, and $190,000 turns on who wins. Findings at a Glance This study should be treated as a proxy for how much humans miss. We kept our analysis deliberately narrow, counting only objective drafting mistakes we could verify from the document itself. We could not judge whether an agreement was signed out of policy, drifted off market, or if a company gave away more than it should, let alone what sits inside the millions of private contracts. These numbers should be thought of as the floor, not a full account of everything worth fixing in an agreement. blogs.title: What Happens to Emails and Side Letters Under an Entire Agreement Clause or Merger Clause?
blogs.author: Harvey Team
blogs.description: Emails, side letters, and sales promises rarely reach the signed contract. Here's how to find them and test each against the entire agreement or merger clause.
blogs.content: Insights What Happens to Emails and Side Letters Under an Entire Agreement Clause or Merger Clause? Emails, side letters, and sales promises rarely reach the signed contract. Here's how to find them and test each against the entire agreement or merger clause. by Harvey Team • Oct 19, 2026 Consider a sales email that promises 24-hour support, in a deal whose Order Form never mentions it. Whether that email still counts depends largely on a single paragraph of boilerplate. That paragraph is the entire agreement clause. It states that the signed contract is the parties' complete agreement on its subject matter, and it supersedes the earlier agreements, proposals, representations, and communications it names. US lawyers usually call the same provision a merger clause or an integration clause. This article describes how to find promises like that one in the deal correspondence and test each against the clause, both before signature and after a dispute. Harvey locates the communications and flags the conflicts, and lawyers decide what they mean under the governing law. Drafting the clause itself is a separate subject, and Harvey's guide to drafting clauses in legal documents is a good place to begin. Delivery Dates, Support Levels, and Pricing Terms get Settled in Email Commercial deals rarely live in one document, which is why the commitments are spread across several places by the time the contract is signed: Email threads hold delivery dates the account team confirmed and support levels the technical team promised during diligence. Term sheets and letters of intent settle pricing conditions that often never reach the long-form draft. Side letters address one customer's requirement while the main agreement stays on the provider's standard form. Requests for proposals (RFPs) and sales decks describe functionality, timing, and service levels that the agreement does not convert into warranties or obligations. Reliance on a message does not make it part of the contract. The signed documents either preserve it, supersede it, incorporate it, or leave its effect to the governing law. Finding the 24-hour support email before signature gives the team a chance to decide whether the commitment belongs in the signed contract. One Vault Holds the Emails, Decks, and Side Letters Together Locating that email by hand means searching inboxes, shared drives, and deal folders. A Vault in Harvey holds up to 100,000 files, including email files and their attachments, so the whole deal can be loaded in one place. Some of the correspondence will still sit in an inbox. With full inbox search turned on, Harvey for Outlook lets a lawyer ask a plain-language question about a deal and then Harvey searches the inbox for the answer. The setting is optional and off by default. Once the correspondence is in, a Review Table converts the messages into rows. Each row captures the sender, recipient, subject, and any commitment the message makes. The 24-hour support promise appears as a single row. With Harvey II, an agent begins each step already holding the deal's documents and history, which removes the need to brief it again. The video below shows the same Review Table approach on a case chronology built from a large email set. Watch Video Three Parts of the Clause Set What to Check for Each Promise With the emails loaded, the clause itself determines what to test. blogs.description: Harvey Graph organizes legal and matter data, maps how it connects, and hands that structure to agents at run time so they deliver high quality, personalized work.
blogs.content: Product Improving Agent Accuracy With Harvey Graph Harvey Graph organizes legal and matter data, maps how it connects, and hands that structure to agents at run time so they deliver high quality, personalized work. by Harvey Team • Oct 19, 2026 If you have used an AI tool for legal work, you know the ritual. Before you can ask your question, you explain the situation. You upload the documents. You describe the client, the deal, and how your partner likes things done. Then you ask. And on the next matter, you do it all again. That routine is changing, in part because models have become much better at legal task execution. We benchmark new models on agentic legal work in Harvey LAB, and the results show how far their capabilities have advanced. When every agent can reason well, what separates them for legal use cases is what they know before they start: context about the matter, the documents, the precedents, your client preferences, and the way your team works. That context is where agent quality succeeds or fails. Harvey Graph helps provide that context. It organizes firm data and legal knowledge and maps how they connect, so an agent starts a task the way a well-briefed teammate would: already knowing your preferences, the project, and the precedents that matter to the work. Watch Video Harvey has spent the past year investing in this context layer of our platform. With the release of Harvey II this month, Spaces provide a closed, private graph of your matter’s data, how it fits together, and how it connects to the people who use it. Additionally, our US Case Law knowledge source uses a graph to map citations and relationships across the body of American case law. We refer to the combination of all these specialized graphs, and the graphs we have in development, as Harvey Graph. Users will never have to know the graph is there or activate it. But they will notice Harvey asking less of them up front, while consistently delivering accurate work that is verifiable with citations. How Harvey Graph Improves Agent Answer Quality Legal work goes beyond being able to read and understand the latest case or draft. It’s highly relational, so agents need to be able to navigate those relationships to deliver accurate outputs. A single credit agreement arrives with drafts, amendments, and side letters, and an agent has to know which version controls before it can answer anything about it. A diligence finding depends on a change-of-control clause, the counterparty it names, and the deal timeline it sits in. Lawyers hold these connections in their heads, and without a graph, agents try to rebuild and assume the connections from raw data and files on every task. Flat retrieval (chunks ranked by similarity) finds passages, not relationships. An agent working this way re-discovers the same entities and cross-references task after task, spending time and tokens to recover structure that was already in the documents. The technical solution sounds simple: better-organized context, a graph that maps the relationships between documents, work product, people, matters, and knowledge. The difficulty is in the word “relationships.” A firm’s data doesn’t announce how it connects. Nothing in a document says it’s the fourth draft of an agreement that was later superseded, that the counterparty in it is the same entity under a different name in another matter, or that the case it relies on was overruled last year. All of those connections have to be inferred, verified against the source, and kept current as the firm’s work changes — across millions of documents and governed by existing permissions and ethical walls. What’s in Harvey Graph Today The main Harvey Agent plans and orchestrates work across the platform. Custom agents handle specialized tasks behind the scenes, so users don’t need to select or manage them. The Harvey Graph works the same way. blogs.author: Harvey Team
blogs.description: A contract playbook only works if it runs on every draft and changes with the results. Here's what Word review flags and when to revise the rules.
blogs.content: Insights Run Your Contract Playbook on Every Draft, Then Refine the Rules A contract playbook only works if it runs on every draft and changes with the results. Here's what Word review flags and when to revise the rules. by Harvey Team • Oct 16, 2026 A contract playbook is the rulebook for one contract type: the positions your team prefers, the fallbacks it will accept, and the point where a deviation goes to a lawyer. In-house legal teams usually own it and apply it to counterparty paper, and some call it a legal playbook. It pays off when the team runs it on every draft and revises it from what those drafts show. Throughout the rest of this article, we'll follow one customer's services agreement, checked against a software company's Playbook, from the first clause to the changes the results send back to the Playbook. Need to pull terms out of hundreds of agreements at once instead? Start with AI contract analysis at scale . Executed Contracts, Old Guidelines, or a Blank Page Can All Seed a Playbook You don't have to start a contract negotiation playbook from a blank table of hypothetical positions. Harvey’s Playbook Builder converts an existing playbook into structured rules, builds rules from contracts that already hold language your team won, or helps you create them from scratch. Executed agreements are especially useful when your written policy and your negotiating history have drifted apart. A good rule carries a preferred position, a fallback, guidance for the reviewer, and an escalation path. Playbook Builder also keeps citations to the source documents behind each rule, so you can check how a standard was built. The hard cases sit between the standard and the fallback. Say your Playbook prefers payment within 30 days and accepts 60. Then "Net 75" lands on your desk. The reviewer needs enough guidance to see why it's out of range and what to do next. You can also mark a rule required, so missing standard language gets flagged. With the rules in place, run them on a live draft. Every Covered Clause Comes Back Acceptable, Needs Review, or Unacceptable Say the incoming draft is a customer's services agreement on the customer's paper. Playbook review in Word checks every covered clause against your rules and shows the result in the draft. Here's how it might come back (illustrative): Clause Incoming language Playbook result Next action Payment terms Net 75 Needs review Fallback allows net 60, so counter at 60 Liability cap Unlimited for data breach Unacceptable Negotiate to the capped position Governing law Delaware Acceptable None Assignment Consent not required for affiliate transfers Needs review Fallback allows affiliate transfers with notice "Acceptable" means the clause fits a position you've already approved. "Needs review" is your queue, and "unacceptable" is your negotiation list. You stay in control either way. After reading Harvey's reasoning, you check the proposed language and accept edits as tracked changes inside Harvey for Word , right where you already draft. No copying clauses into another tool. In Practice: For Carvana, scaling playbooks with Harvey reduced drafting and review time by 80%. Read how the Playbook Builder works . Want to see it in action? Millie Lehmann, Strategic Business Development Lead at Harvey, builds a Playbook from existing guidelines and runs it against a live contract in Word. Watch Video See how a Playbook moves from existing guidance into a live contract review in Harvey for Word. Provisions Nobody Wrote a Rule for Still Get Flagged for Review Your Playbook only knows what your team has written down, and counterparty paper keeps wandering into positions nobody planned for. In our example, the customer's data-use clause matches no rule at all. Harvey flags it for manual review because no rule covers it, and the lawyer decides whether the clause is acceptable. blogs.title: Regulatory Consent Order Compliance Depends on a Remediation Record That Outlasts the Team
blogs.author: Harvey Team
blogs.description: A consent order commits you to fixes, deadlines, and proof. Here's how legal maps each paragraph to an owner and keeps the evidence behind it together.
blogs.content: Insights Regulatory Consent Order Compliance Depends on a Remediation Record That Outlasts the Team A consent order commits you to fixes, deadlines, and proof. Here's how legal maps each paragraph to an owner and keeps the evidence behind it together. by Harvey Team • Oct 16, 2026 A consent order can outlast the team that negotiated it. By the final report, the lawyer filing it may never have met the people who shaped the original terms. A durable remediation record connects the current team to the decisions and evidence that came before it. A regulatory consent order is a binding order, entered with the respondent's consent, that requires specific corrective actions by set deadlines. Depending on the proceeding, a regulator or a court enters it. Duration varies. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC), for example, ordinarily ends its administrative orders in consumer protection and competition matters after 20 years under a 1995 sunset policy (60 Fed. Reg. 42,569). That policy does not cover federal court orders, and other regulators set their own terms. Keeping that record usable for years takes close reading of the order and a clear link from every commitment to its proof. Legal AI can take on much of that reading. Harvey can structure the order paragraph by paragraph, mapping each commitment to its deadline and the evidence the team expects to use to show completion. The work lives in one place, so the next team picks up where the last one stopped. This article follows one order from receipt to closure and shows where Harvey supports the work at each stage. Teams still turning new regulations into policies and controls should start with compliance management. Responding to the original notice of violation and tracking contractual obligations after signature are separate jobs with separate records. Each Operative Paragraph Becomes a Commitment With a Deadline and Proof A long order mixes findings, definitions, recitals, and operative provisions. Findings record what the regulator concluded, and definitions control how the rest of the order reads. Only the operative paragraphs tell the respondent what to do. Harvey breaks dense regulatory text into obligations, deadlines, and the responsible parties the text names , so the team can work from those paragraphs. A Review Table gives that work a shape: one row for each operative commitment, in the order's own words, with its deadline and the evidence expected to show completion. Ambiguous terms go to a review queue, where a lawyer resolves them before anyone builds a task on a guess. A simplified example follows: Order paragraph Commitment Internal owner Deadline Evidence of completion Revise the consumer complaint policy and obtain required approval Update and approve the complaint-handling policy Compliance Date stated in the order Approved policy and board or committee minutes Train covered employees on the revised procedure Complete required training Compliance and Human Resources Date stated in the order Training materials and completion records Submit periodic compliance report Prepare and file the report Legal and Compliance Reporting date in the order Filed report and supporting source documents The order establishes what the respondent owes. The organization decides who carries each commitment out. Harvey helps structure the commitments, and Legal and Compliance assign the owners. Every Remediation Item Should Trace Back to the Paragraph it Answers With the order mapped, the remediation plan should be checked in both directions. Each operative commitment needs at least one plan item, and each plan item should answer a specific paragraph. A plan that traces back to the order is easier to defend. A remediation plan may build on policies and controls the organization already has in place, and a gap analysis shows what remains. If a complaint policy already meets four of five required elements, the task is to close the fifth gap and document the change. Depending on the order,

blogs.title: How GCs are Rethinking Legal Work With AI
blogs.author: Harvey Team
blogs.description: Three in-house leaders share how they’re expanding their teams’ capacity while keeping lawyers’ judgment central to the work.
blogs.content: Insights How GCs are Rethinking Legal Work With AI Three in-house leaders share how they’re expanding their teams’ capacity while keeping lawyers’ judgment central to the work. by Harvey Team • Oct 16, 2026 In-house legal teams face a steady stream of work that varies in urgency, complexity, and the judgment required. AI can accelerate first drafts and other preparatory work, giving lawyers more room to focus on decisions that require their deep knowledge of the business. That raises an important question for legal leaders: Which work should the team take on vs. hand off to AI, and where can its lawyers add the most value? At Harvey FORUM in Sydney, Silv Roest, Group Chief Legal, Corporate Affairs, and Sustainability Officer at The Warehouse Group; Andrew Chivers, Regional General Counsel, APAC at Brambles Limited; and Georgette Apostolopoulos, General Counsel at The Star shared what they’re learning as AI becomes part of their teams’ day-to-day work. Their examples offer practical lessons for using AI to change how legal teams work, beyond accelerating individual tasks. Change How the Work is Divided At The Warehouse Group, one of the largest retailing groups in New Zealand, Roest is looking at how a four-lawyer team spends its time. First drafts, summaries, and issue tables are necessary work, but they can make it difficult to reach the questions that need the team’s judgment and knowledge of the business. That makes the division of work a useful place to start. Watch Video Apostolopoulos faced a different capacity challenge at The Star, one of Australia’s leading integrated resort companies. After the legal team downsized, it no longer had an in-house litigator to run an anti-discrimination matter. Her team used AI to help prepare the evidence before asking outside firms for quotes. By preparing the evidence in-house, the team could ask firms to price the work that remained, giving it a way to manage outside counsel costs. Watch Video Both examples start by breaking work into its component steps. Legal leaders can then identify what AI can help prepare, where their lawyers need to apply judgment, and when outside counsel’s expertise is needed. That gives a lean team a clearer way to allocate its time and scope external work. Make Existing Knowledge Easier to Use For a legal team supporting a global business, even a familiar question can take time to answer when the relevant guidance sits across different policies and jurisdictions. Global supply chain logistics company Brambles has 24 lawyers working across 60 countries. Chivers described how his team brought its policies together in an agent that people can query, reducing the need to search through documents each time a question comes in. Watch Video The example offers a useful starting point for teams with knowledge spread across many documents: look for questions that come up repeatedly and require lawyers to consult the same sources. Making those sources easier to use can help the team respond more quickly, while lawyers still assess how the guidance applies to the particular situation. Help Lawyers Evaluate AI Output Making information easier to access also changes the skills lawyers need to practice. Chivers noted that junior lawyers may be comfortable using AI while still developing the legal knowledge needed to challenge its answers. Familiarity with the tool is useful; the ability to spot a missing fact, weak inference, or incorrect conclusion takes training. Watch Video That training can happen in the course of real work. When reviewing an AI-assisted draft, a supervising lawyer can ask a junior colleague what they checked, where the answer came from, and why they agree with it. The discussion helps the junior lawyer develop judgment alongside their ability to use the tool. blogs.author: Harvey Team
blogs.description: Legal Work Orchestration brings the phases, tasks, and reviews of a matter or project into the same place as the documents and the agents.
blogs.content: Product Making Harvey the Orchestration Layer for Legal Work Legal Work Orchestration brings the phases, tasks, and reviews of a matter or project into the same place as the documents and the agents. by Harvey Team • Oct 15, 2026 Today, we’re launching Legal Work Orchestration , a new way to organize and manage legal matters in Harvey. It connects the phases, tasks, people, and review points within a matter so that agents can execute defined tasks, lawyers can review their work at designated gates, and everyone involved can see what needs to happen next. Watch Video Much of legal work follows a repeatable process. An M&A transaction, for example, moves through familiar phases, tasks, and review points. But the process itself often has to be reconstructed for every new matter from a checklist, a previous deal, or the knowledge of the people who have done it before. AI agents can already complete many individual steps within that process. What they often lack is the structure around the task: where it fits in the matter, which documents and instructions apply, who should review the output, and what happens next. Lawyers still have to provide that context, move the work between people and systems, and track its progress. Legal Work Orchestration brings that structure into Harvey, allowing lawyers and agents to work through a matter together in one place. How Legal Orchestration Works The same structure can support any matter or project a team runs more than once, from an M&A transaction to a quarterly compliance review. Legal Work Orchestration captures that process in a reusable template, carries the relevant context into each task, and coordinates reviews and next steps. Capture the Process in a Reusable Template Templates capture how your organization runs a recurring type of work. When an associate opens a new buy-side acquisition, the Space can already contain the relevant phases, tasks, playbooks, agents, collaborators, and review gates. Innovation and knowledge teams can define that structure once, helping teams follow a consistent process across matters without rebuilding it from scratch. Give Every Task the Context it Needs Each task includes its scope, inputs, and reviewer. An agent assigned a change-of-control review can therefore analyze the relevant contracts and produce a consent matrix without the lawyer having to assemble a new prompt and briefing for that step. Tasks can also be assigned to another lawyer or shared with the client while retaining the relevant matter context. The work no longer depends on one person manually carrying information from one step to the next. Keep Reviews and Next Steps Moving When the agent completes the review, Harvey notifies the designated partner that the consent matrix is ready. Once the partner approves it, the task is completed and the next step can begin. Updates can also be made from email. A lawyer can ask Harvey in a reply to close a task or begin the next one, while the Space maintains a current view of the matter’s progress. Partners can see where the work stands without asking an associate to reconstruct the status from email and separate checklists. The Future of Legal Work Orchestration Before the release of Harvey II in August, every step delegated to Harvey required a lawyer to gather the documents, write the instructions, and move the output to wherever it needed to go next. Legal Work Orchestration reduces that overhead by giving each task its inputs, instructions, and reviewer in advance. Today, lawyers still actively prompt the majority of steps in a legal workflow. We expect that balance to change rapidly. Over the next six months, we expect agents to take on an additional 20% of workflow steps. Within a year, we expect that share to triple. Lawyers will remain in control through defined review gates, and the work performed by agents will remain transparent and auditable. But as agents take on more of the execution, lawyers will be able to focus more of their a
